content:
A new study details SimpleDesign, a streamlined AI model from Apple researchers capable of jointly generating protein sequences and structures. Here's the rundown.

Some background

Last September, Apple researchers published a study titled "SimpleFold: Folding Proteins is Easier than You Think," detailing a simplified method for predicting a protein's three-dimensional structure from its amino acid sequence.

In short, SimpleFold uses flow matching models to generate a protein's 3D structure directly from its amino acid sequence.

We previously explained flow matching in detail, but in brief, it's a technique that learns a relatively direct path from a noisy random starting point to the final result. In contrast, diffusion models typically arrive at their final output through iterative denoising.

Both techniques are most commonly (or at least traditionally) associated with image generation, though researchers (including Apple's) have explored diffusion models for text and code generation as well.

Returning to SimpleFold, Apple essentially combined flow matching with general-purpose Transformer blocks (more commonly used in text generation), allowing the model to avoid some of the more computationally expensive techniques often used by protein-folding models (such as DeepMind's well-known system, AlphaFold).

Now, Apple researchers have published SimpleDesign, extending the simplified, general-purpose architectural ideas they explored in SimpleFold to the broader task of protein design—not just predicting a protein's 3D structure.

SimpleDesign

As Apple researchers explain in their new study, "SimpleDesign: A Protein Sequence and Structure Joint-Design Model":

That is, while many existing protein design models rely on multi-stage pipelines, SimpleDesign can learn to jointly generate amino acid sequences and continuous 3D structures in a single end-to-end training process.

Many existing protein co-design models work like this: first, a separate model is trained to convert protein structures into discrete representations, or "tokens"; then a generative model is trained on these representations to generate new protein sequences and structures.

SimpleDesign skips this intermediate step, learning directly from paired amino acid sequence and 3D coordinate data, rather than first compressing protein structures into a separate, tokenized representation.

The way Apple researchers trained SimpleDesign is quite interesting.

They started with more than 2 million paired protein sequence and structure samples, primarily from the AFESM dataset, which combines predicted structures from the AlphaFold database with additional samples.

During training, they simultaneously perturbed both parts of each pair: amino acids in the sequence were randomly masked out, and noise was added to the corresponding 3D structures.

The researchers also varied the degree of corruption on both sides. If the sequence was mostly intact but the structure was heavily corrupted, the task resembled protein folding—the model had to recover the structure from a known sequence.

Conversely, if the structure was mostly intact but the sequence was heavily masked, it resembled inverse folding. The model had to generate sequences capable of producing a given structure.

When both sides were partially corrupted, the model had to tackle both problems simultaneously—which is essentially training it for protein co-design.

According to the results, SimpleDesign achieved competitive performance on benchmarks for protein co-design, structure generation, and sequence generation, despite its significantly simplified training pipeline.

The researchers also found that SimpleDesign can generate plausible protein structures, and the amino acid sequences it produces generally match or surpass those from most competing multimodal models.

Finally, the researchers note that SimpleDesign's results are currently limited to computational evaluation, because the generated proteins have not been experimentally tested to confirm they actually fold, function, or operate safely in real biological systems.

Even so, the results are quite encouraging, and the full study (which of course explores SimpleDesign's architecture, training process, benchmarks, and results in much greater depth) is well worth a read.
